exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect HIVAN over TB‑related renal disease? — Look for nephrotic‑range proteinuria, bland urine sediment, and rapid eGFR decline without active urinary casts.
A patient with HIV, CD4 150, presents with edema and proteinuria. What is your next step? — Initiate ART urgently, start ACE‑I/ARB, and arrange renal function monitoring.
How does the presence of APOL1 risk alleles influence management? — Recognize higher risk of rapid progression; prioritize early ART and strict blood pressure control.

If a kidney biopsy is unavailable, how do you confirm HIVAN? — Use clinical criteria (proteinuria >1 g/day, eGFR <60, HIV uncontrolled) and exclude other glomerulopathies with serology and urine microscopy.
Why might serum creatinine be misleading early in HIVAN? — Hyperfiltration can keep creatinine normal despite structural damage; trend over time is more informative.
What drug interactions must you watch when starting tenofovir in a patient with reduced eGFR? — Adjust dose if eGFR 30‑50, avoid concomitant nephrotoxic NSAIDs, and monitor for phosphatemia.
When is corticosteroid therapy appropriate in HIVAN? — Only in biopsy‑proven collapsing FSGS with severe proteinuria and after infectious causes are controlled, due to infection risk.

How do you differentiate HIVAN from hepatitis B‑associated membranous nephropathy? — HIVAN shows collapsing lesions and bland sediment; hepatitis B often has immune complex deposits and positive HBsAg with membranous pattern on biopsy.
ai.title: HIV-Associated Nephropathy
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN) is a collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis seen in untreated HIV infection, especially in people of African descent. It presents with proteinuria, edema, and rapid renal decline. Diagnosis relies on clinical features and kidney biopsy when available.

b: Kidney biopsy (if feasible) showing collapsing FSGS
sections.p: HIVAN is a kidney disease caused by direct infection of renal epithelial cells by HIV, leading to collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Diagnosis requires proteinuria >1 g/day, reduced eGFR, and exclusion of other causes; biopsy shows collapse of glomerular tufts and tubular microcystic change.

t.b: Detects presence of proteinuria; a +2 or greater suggests >1 g/day and warrants further quantification.

Assesses renal function; eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates moderate CKD.
Looks for enlarged kidneys and loss of corticomedullary differentiation; helps rule out obstruction when biopsy unavailable.
Confirms collapsing FSGS; if unavailable, rely on clinical pattern and exclusion of other diseases.

sections.p: Staging follows KDIGO CKD categories based on eGFR and albuminuria, guiding prognosis and timing of referral.

sections.p: HIVAN results from direct viral injury, host genetics (APOL1 risk alleles), and immune activation. Co‑existing infections and nephrotoxic exposures common in low‑resource settings accelerate damage.
Patients develop painless edema, often periorbital or lower‑leg, with frothy urine. Rapid rise in serum creatinine over weeks to months is typical. Hypertension may be mild or absent.
Focus on quantifying protein loss, assessing renal function, and ruling out other glomerulopathies.

sections.p: Treat HIV aggressively, control proteinuria, and avoid nephrotoxins. Use ACE inhibitors or ARBs for renoprotection; start ART promptly, adjusting for renal dosing when needed.
